Formal public school **Education in [West Virginia](West_Virginia "West Virginia")** falls under the auspices of the [West Virginia Department of Education](West_Virginia_Department_of_Education "West Virginia Department of Education"). Each county in West Virginia constitutes a school district.

## Education administration

### West Virginia Board of Education

The **West Virginia Board of Education** is established in the West Virginia Constitution. The Board is vested with general supervision of West Virginia's 834 elementary and secondary schools. Its twelve members include nine citizens appointed by the governor and three non-voting ex-officio members: the State Superintendent of Schools, the Chancellor of the West Virginia Higher Education Policy Commission, and the Chancellor of Community and Technical Education. The State Superintendent is a constitutional officer who serves at the will of the board. Board members serve overlapping terms of nine years, and no more than five citizen members may belong to the same political party.

The West Virginia Board of Education meets monthly to determine the educational policies of the elementary and secondary schools and to establish the rules that carry into effect state law regarding education. The State Board of Education also has general control, supervision, and management of the business and educational affairs of the [West Virginia Schools for the Deaf and Blind](West_Virginia_Schools_for_the_Deaf_and_Blind "West Virginia Schools for the Deaf and Blind") in [Romney](Romney%2C_West_Virginia "Romney, West Virginia").

# Multi-Agent Delegation

When the user asks a complex question, do not attempt to answer it yourself. Break it up into smaller pieces, then use the `fork` tool to delegate each piece to a subagent. You MUST use the `join` tool to retrieve the subagent's result for each subagent you create with `fork`. Each subagent has access to the exact same tools that you do.

If you are confident you can answer the user's query without help, do not use the delegation tools.

## Writing Instructions

The instructions you give to each subagent SHOULD be a smaller piece of the instructions you were given. Do not delegate your full task to a subagent. Subagents do not have access to the information you have retrieved in prior turns or your thoughts. You must provide each subagent with the necessary context it needs in its instructions.

Your instructions to a subagent can be long, up to about 5000 characters. Each subagent is as capable as you are, but starts with a blank slate, so you must provide it specific and detailed information in its instructions.

There are 60 colleges and universities in the U.S. state of <Alabama>. The [University of Alabama](University_of_Alabama "University of Alabama") in [Tuscaloosa](Tuscaloosa%2C_Alabama "Tuscaloosa, Alabama") is the largest university in the state with 38,100 enrolled for fall 2019.[[1]](List_of_colleges_and_universities_in_Alabama#cite_note-UA_2010_enrollment-1) [Jefferson State Community College](Jefferson_State_Community_College "Jefferson State Community College") in [Birmingham, Alabama](Birmingham%2C_Alabama "Birmingham, Alabama") is the largest two-year college, with an enrollment of just over 8,000. The smallest institution is [Heritage Christian University](Heritage_Christian_University "Heritage Christian University"), a [Churches of Christ](Churches_of_Christ "Churches of Christ")-affiliated [seminary](Seminary "Seminary"), with an enrollment of 86 students. The oldest institution is [Athens State University](Athens_State_University "Athens State University") in [Athens](Athens%2C_Alabama "Athens, Alabama") founded in 1822.[[2]](List_of_colleges_and_universities_in_Alabama#cite_note-athens-2) There are also 8 four-year and 3 two-year [historically black colleges and universities](Historically_black_colleges_and_universities "Historically black colleges and universities") which is more than any other state.[[3]](List_of_colleges_and_universities_in_Alabama#cite_note-histblack-3)

The majority of Alabama's colleges and universities are accredited by the [Southern Association of Colleges and Schools](Southern_Association_of_Colleges_and_Schools "Southern Association of Colleges and Schools") (SACS),[[4]](List_of_colleges_and_universities_in_Alabama#cite_note-SACS_list-4) although several are accredited by the [Association for Biblical Higher Education](Association_for_Biblical_Higher_Education "Association for Biblical Higher Education") (ABHE),[[5]](List_of_colleges_and_universities_in_Alabama#cite_note-5) the [Council on Occupational Education](Council_on_Occupational_Education "Council on Occupational Education") (COE),[[6]](List_of_colleges_and_universities_in_Alabama#cite_note-6) or the [Distance Education Accrediting Commission](Distance_Education_Accrediting_Commission "Distance Education Accrediting Commission") (DEAC).

The [University of Alabama at Birmingham](University_of_Alabama_School_of_Medicine "University of Alabama School of Medicine"), the [University of South Alabama](University_of_South_Alabama "University of South Alabama"), the [Alabama College of Osteopathic Medicine](Alabama_College_of_Osteopathic_Medicine "Alabama College of Osteopathic Medicine"), and the [Edward Via College of Osteopathic Medicine](Edward_Via_College_of_Osteopathic_Medicine "Edward Via College of Osteopathic Medicine") feature the only medical schools in the state.[[7]](List_of_colleges_and_universities_in_Alabama#cite_note-7) The [University of Alabama School of Law](University_of_Alabama_School_of_Law "University of Alabama School of Law"), the [Cumberland School of Law](Cumberland_School_of_Law "Cumberland School of Law") at [Samford University](Samford_University "Samford University"), and the [Thomas Goode Jones School of Law](Thomas_Goode_Jones_School_of_Law "Thomas Goode Jones School of Law") at [Faulkner University](Faulkner_University "Faulkner University") are [American Bar Association](American_Bar_Association "American Bar Association")-accredited law schools.[[8]](List_of_colleges_and_universities_in_Alabama#cite_note-8) The [Birmingham School of Law](Birmingham_School_of_Law "Birmingham School of Law") and [Miles Law School](Miles_Law_School "Miles Law School") (unaffiliated with [Miles College](Miles_College "Miles College")) are state accredited law programs.[[9]](List_of_colleges_and_universities_in_Alabama#cite_note-9)

There are four institutions of higher learning in Alabama that are listed among Tier 1 national universities by U.S. News & World Report - The University of Alabama (UA), Auburn University (AU), the University of Alabama at Birmingham (UAB), and The University of Alabama in Huntsville (UAH).

These four universities are also [classified](Carnegie_Classification_of_Institutions_of_Higher_Education "Carnegie Classification of Institutions of Higher Education") among "R1: Doctoral Universities – Very high research activity: "The University of Alabama, The University of Alabama at Birmingham, The University of Alabama in Huntsville, and Auburn University as of February 2022.

The **Alabama Community College System** (**ACCS**) is the [system](State_university_system "State university system") of [public](Public_university "Public university") [community colleges](Community_college "Community college") in the U.S. state of <Alabama>. It consists of 24 community and technical colleges in the state which offer 2-to-4-year transfer, dual enrollment, technical training, adult education, and community education.[[4]](Alabama_Community_College_System#cite_note-accs_homepage-4)

The Alabama Community College System was founded 1963 when the public two-year colleges in Alabama were linked into a single system governed by the State Board of Education. The system was separated from the State Board of Education and put under control of the Department of Postsecondary Education in 1982.[[1]](Alabama_Community_College_System#cite_note-accs_history-1)

Based on my research of Wikipedia articles about Alabama's higher education system, I found comprehensive information about public colleges and universities in Alabama. Here's what I discovered:

## Count of Public Colleges and Universities in Alabama

According to the Wikipedia article "List of colleges and universities in Alabama," there are **60 total colleges and universities** in the state, with **39 being public institutions**.

### Breakdown of Public Institutions:

**Public 4-Year Universities (15):**
1. Air University (US Air Force)
2. Alabama A&M University
3. Alabama State University
4. Athens State University
5. Auburn University
6. Auburn University at Montgomery
7. Jacksonville State University
8. Troy University
9. University of Alabama
10. University of Alabama at Birmingham (UAB)
11. University of Alabama in Huntsville (UAH)
12. University of Montevallo
13. University of North Alabama
14. University of South Alabama
15. University of West Alabama

**Public Community and Technical Colleges (24):**
These are organized under the **Alabama Community College System (ACCS)**, which was founded in 1963 and consists of 24 community and technical colleges across the state. These include Bevill State, Bishop State, Calhoun Community College, Central Alabama Community College, Chattahoochee Valley, Coastal Alabama, Enterprise State, Gadsden State, and others throughout the state.

### Key Facts:
- **Total institutions in Alabama:** 60 colleges and universities
- **Public institutions:** 39 (15 four-year universities + 24 community/technical colleges)
- **Private institutions:** 21 (the remainder)
- Alabama has more historically black colleges and universities (HBCUs) than any other state, with 8 four-year and 3 two-year HBCUs

The Alabama Commission on Higher Education serves as the statewide agency responsible for coordinating higher education in Alabama and overseeing these public institutions.

The **education system in <Mississippi>** consists of [elementary](Elementary_school "Elementary school"), [middle](Middle_school "Middle school"), and [high schools](High_school "High school") as well as [boarding schools](Boarding_school "Boarding school"), [public](State_school "State school") and [private schools](Private_school "Private school"), and [colleges](College "College") and [universities](Universities "Universities").

Mississippi has a reputation of having the lowest ranked education system in the [United States](United_States "United States"). In 2008, Mississippi ranked last in academic achievement by the [American Legislative Exchange Council](American_Legislative_Exchange_Council "American Legislative Exchange Council")'s Report Card on Education with the lowest average [ACT](ACT_(test) "ACT (test)") score[[1]](Public_Education_in_Mississippi#cite_note-1) and the 6th lowest spending per pupil in the nation. On the other hand, by 2019 Mississippi had significantly narrowed the gap in the [National Assessment of Educational Progress](National_Assessment_of_Educational_Progress "National Assessment of Educational Progress"), even achieving parity for both reading[[2]](Public_Education_in_Mississippi#cite_note-2) and mathematics.[[3]](Public_Education_in_Mississippi#cite_note-3)

Most of the schools in Mississippi are accredited by the [Southern Association of Colleges and Schools](Southern_Association_of_Colleges_and_Schools "Southern Association of Colleges and Schools").

## K-12

### Mississippi Department of Education

The Mississippi Board of Education has nine appointed members, and they appoint the State Superintendent of Education who sets educational policies and oversees the [Mississippi Department of Education](Mississippi_Department_of_Education "Mississippi Department of Education"). The Mississippi Governor appoints one member of the Board of Education from Mississippi's Northern Supreme Court District, one from the Central Supreme Court District, one from the Southern Supreme Court District, one employed school administrator, and one employed public school teacher. The Lieutenant Governor appoints two members-at-large, and the Speaker of the Mississippi House of Representatives appoints two members-at-large.

The Mississippi Board of Education divides the Department of Education into functioning divisions and is responsible for establishing and maintaining their policy system and designing and maintaining curriculum for public school students that prepares them for the work force. They are also responsible for regulating curriculum, teacher standards and certification, student testing, accountability, school accreditation and any other problems that arise in the school system.

### Demographics

In Mississippi, there are 152 [school districts](School_district "School district") consisting of 3 agricultural high schools, 68 county unit districts, and 81 separate district schools.

There are 1,089 elementary and secondary schools with 491,962 students and 33,358 teachers, compared to the national averages of 1,999 schools, 965,991 students, and 63,179 teachers. The pupil to teach ratio in Mississippi is 14.7, compared to the national average of 15.3.

### Educational Programs

The Office of Vocational Education and Workforce Development prepares students for the workforce by providing them with programs to teach them about various fields in business and industry. It is an integrated educational delivery system that provides programs for secondary (middle and high school), postsecondary (college), and short-term adult programs.

[Mississippi Public Broadcasting](Mississippi_Public_Broadcasting "Mississippi Public Broadcasting") (MPB) was signed on air with its first broadcast on February 1, 1970. It began airing radio programs in 1984. It reaches 2.2 million households in Mississippi, and 127,000 Mississippians listen to its radio programming weekly. 40% of its programming is geared towards children.

### Specialized Schools

The [Mississippi School for the Deaf](Mississippi_School_for_the_Deaf "Mississippi School for the Deaf") is the state residential school for students who are deaf and hard of hearing. It is located in the state's capital of [Jackson, Mississippi](Jackson%2C_Mississippi "Jackson, Mississippi"), and it was founded in 1854.

The [Mississippi School for Mathematics and Science](Mississippi_School_for_Mathematics_and_Science "Mississippi School for Mathematics and Science") (MSMS) is a public residential school for gifted students located in [Columbus, Mississippi](Columbus%2C_Mississippi "Columbus, Mississippi") on the campus of the [Mississippi University for Women](Mississippi_University_for_Women "Mississippi University for Women"). The **Mississippi Community College Board** (MCCB), formerly the **Mississippi State Board for Community and Junior Colleges** (SBCJC), is a statutory coordinating board tasked with oversight of the public community and junior colleges of the state of [Mississippi](Mississippi_(U.S._state) "Mississippi (U.S. state)").

## Institutions

Board members are appointed for staggered terms by the [Governor of Mississippi](Governor_of_Mississippi "Governor of Mississippi") to oversee 15 schools.

- [Coahoma Community College](Coahoma_Community_College "Coahoma Community College")
- [Copiah-Lincoln Community College](Copiah-Lincoln_Community_College "Copiah-Lincoln Community College")
- [East Central Community College](East_Central_Community_College "East Central Community College")
- [East Mississippi Community College](East_Mississippi_Community_College "East Mississippi Community College")
- [Hinds Community College](Hinds_Community_College "Hinds Community College")
- [Holmes Community College](Holmes_Community_College "Holmes Community College")
- [Itawamba Community College](Itawamba_Community_College "Itawamba Community College")
- [Jones County Junior College](Jones_County_Junior_College "Jones County Junior College")

- [Mississippi Delta Community College](Mississippi_Delta_Community_College "Mississippi Delta Community College")
- [Mississippi Gulf Coast Community College](Mississippi_Gulf_Coast_Community_College "Mississippi Gulf Coast Community College")
- [Northeast Mississippi Community College](Northeast_Mississippi_Community_College "Northeast Mississippi Community College")
- [Northwest Mississippi Community College](Northwest_Mississippi_Community_College "Northwest Mississippi Community College")
- [Pearl River Community College](Pearl_River_Community_College "Pearl River Community College")
- [Southwest Mississippi Community College](Southwest_Mississippi_Community_College "Southwest Mississippi Community College")


Each of the institutions offers dual enrollment and dual credit courses in conjunction with local high schools, adult education programs that lead to a High School Equivalency credential, career and technical programs of study that are designed to prepare students for immediate entry to the local workforce, university transfer programs that prepare students for transfer success at four-year institutions of higher learning, and non-credit programs focused on specific workforce-related needs identified in each community where a community college is located. Many institutions also offer opportunities for interested individuals to take advantage of continuing and community education courses created to teach specific and interesting topics in a non-credit environment. Additionally, students have access to the Mississippi Virtual Community College, which enables students to take courses, via distance learning, at any of the 15 community colleges and receive support from a nearby college.

## History

The Legislature created the board in 1986 to receive and distribute funds from the state, federal government, and other sources to the community and junior colleges.
The initiation of the SBCJC can be traced back to the 1920s. Senate Bill 131, Laws of 1928, approved April 26, 1928, authorized the establishment of junior colleges, and also created a State Commission for oversight of these institutions. The first action of the Commission consisted of identifying its authority, establishing standards by which existing junior colleges must meet to qualify for state aid and develop criteria required of agricultural high schools seeking junior college status. This action of the Commission constituted the birth of Mississippi State System of Public Junior Colleges, giving Mississippi the distinction of having the first state system of comprehensive two-year colleges in the nation. The Commission had no staff but was served by personnel within the State Department of Education. In 1968, a separate operational division for junior colleges was created in the State Department of Education, which provided state services and oversight until 1986.

## Virtual Community College

The Mississippi Virtual Community College (MSVCC) is a [consortium](Consortium "Consortium") of the 15 physical community colleges in the Mississippi system that allows students to take classes over the Internet from any community college located in the state. After almost three years of research and planning, MSVCC was inaugurated in January 2000 under the MCCB Distance Learning program, and currently serves over 20,000 students each semester.
